proposed_line_text: L270: 1. **Structure first: Composite vs. Modifier (Sections 2 and 3).** A coordinated disease-name span is a **Composite Mention**. A single disease name used as a prenominal premodifier, including gene-nomenclature names, deficit-named disorders, and relative-directed phrases where the disease is a premodifier, is a **Modifier**. Whether a disease span is a premodifier or a referential head is decided by the Disease Span Role Rule. A Modifier span is never relabeled under Section 1, the anchor-free compound rule, the individuating-anchor rule, the reference-frame rule, the deficit-named rule, the unqualified generic rule, or the pathological-state rules.

proposed_line_text: L227: **Prenominal disease names.** A multiword disease name, or an abbreviation whose expansion names a disease defined earlier in the text, that directly precedes a head noun is annotated as **Modifier**, provided the span is not coordinated (Section 2). The head noun and any following nomenclature tokens are left unannotated. This applies whether the head denotes a clinical or population entity (e.g., “ovarian cancer cases,” “fragile X syndrome patients”) or a gene, protein, or gene symbol (e.g., “ancient SLS genes,” where “SLS” is defined earlier in the abstract; “breast cancer susceptibility gene 1,” where “breast cancer” is the Modifier and “susceptibility gene 1” is not annotated). Do not infer that the disease span is O merely because the whole noun phrase names a gene or protein. Adjectival forms such as “G6PD deficient phenotype” are also **Modifiers** (see Section 1, rule B(i)). Deficit-named disorders used prenominally (e.g., “C7 deficiency patients”) are likewise **Modifiers**.

raw_reference_text: Section 1 - Deficiency-type nominals with a molecular complement (Rule B, span policy)
proposed_line_text: L101: **Span policy.** Subject to the of-argument boundary below, the preposition does not block or shorten the span. Premodifiers of the molecular name (e.g., “complement component” in “deficiency of complement component C7”) are inside the span. Determiners and descriptors of the head state (e.g., “the,” “complete,” “heterozygous”) are outside it. A parenthetical abbreviation that directly follows the complement, at the end of the nominal, is part of the span (e.g., “deficiency of [enzyme name] (ABBR)” when the conditions hold; Example 41). This trailing-acronym policy is applied uniformly to every deficit-named span. A parenthetical between the molecular name and the head is an interruption (Rule A; What NOT 6) and is not included.

proposed_line_text: L227: **Prenominal disease names.** A multiword disease name, or an abbreviation whose expansion names a disease defined earlier in the text, that directly precedes a head noun is annotated as **Modifier**, provided the span is not coordinated (Section 2). The head noun and any following nomenclature tokens are left unannotated. This applies whether the head denotes a clinical or population entity (e.g., “ovarian cancer cases,” “fragile X syndrome patients”) or a gene, protein, or gene symbol (e.g., “ancient SLS genes,” where “SLS” is defined earlier in the abstract; “breast cancer susceptibility gene 1,” where “breast cancer” is the Modifier and “susceptibility gene 1” is not annotated). Do not infer that the disease span is O merely because the whole noun phrase names a gene or protein. Adjectival forms such as “G6PD deficient phenotype” are also **Modifiers** (see Section 1, rule B(i)). Deficit-named disorders used prenominally (e.g., “C7 deficiency patients”) are likewise **Modifiers**.
